Author: @CaitlinWilliams-i2j
Content:
Appalachian born and raised here, living up in the mountains mostly alone as a new mom really opens your eyes to how these stories come about. It’s easy to think you see shapes among the trees, mistake the regular forest critters scavenging at night for someone hiding just out of sight. 

Some animals make sounds that sound like women and children being murdered. Deer snort and stomp to warn you from coming closer. 

My best advice? If you’re outside alone at night, be LOUD. LOUDDDDD. The last thing you want to do is sneak up on an animal, and most are startled away by loud sounds coming from a distance. 

Also, it’s a “holler”🙂

Ps: if it suddenly gets so quiet that you notice it audibly, leave the area immediately and seek shelter. It’s either something much bigger and scarier than you, or the weather is going to take a nasty turn.

Content:
That kind of stonewall was built in Sweden along fields. The stones that were in the field needed to be removed and since this was loooong before machines and some stones were large and heavy, they didn’t transport them further than necessary and just put them next to the field. Author: @haydnbraun5950
Content: I have worked in the outdoor industry  from Alaska to Florida and gotta say I disagree with a bit of this. I have also guided extensively from FL to VA. My opinion is people underestimate how tricky navigation can be in these places. You can be close to a highway or city and hike up and 15  minutes later feel like you're in the middle of nowhere. I have also guided a lot in CO, UT, WY, CA, and WA.  A lot of national parks and hiking areas in theses states can be more vast but have enough elevation to be above the tree line which helps significantly. Or just not have vegetation like trees or bushes to block your view.  It is hard to get above treeline in Appalachia. I have friends who have done the triple crown. Hiked the AT, CDT, and PCT. Almost every one of them have agreed that the AT (Appalachian trail) is harder than the other two, which on the surface brings greater challenges to overcome.  The population from GA to PA is significantly more than the other 3 thru hikes, and typically encompass more people who are less familiar with outdoor survival and navigation skills. I feel as though this is a fairly reasonable explanation as to how and why a lot of these disappearances and people getting lost happen. Regardless, I do enjoy true crime stuff and do find it fascinating. Especially Stories like these where it does seem that other explanations could be found due to mysterious unknown characters. I would encourage everyone to take a basic nav course, or just look the skills up on a short video on YouTube. I could save your and other people's that you care about life

Content: 28:13 born and raised in Ky. The big cat you are talking about we call it a “screaming Lou” lol. I don’t know why the old timers decided to call it Lou instead of screaming Cindy but yeah they are 100pct around Ky and I have heard people say they have seen them in WV and NC. I heard stories since I was a kid, my grandpa seen one and said his grandpa was riding a covered wagon and a big cat jumped from a tree and destroyed the cover trying to get inside. I seen one late one night driving on a side road deep in the stick “2 joint road” me and my cousin were driving smoking and I dropped the doob out the window when I went to ash it. I got out and was looking on the road as my cousin backed up I would look up at him and motion him to keep backing up. After 2 min tops I seen glowing eyes behind the car, I could see the outline of the big cat it was atleast 6’ long counting its tail, it walked side to side watching me as I stood froze in place. Finally I ran to the car and hopped in and yelled at my cousin to drive. When I told him what I seen he stopped and rolled the windows down and we could hear the cat run up a huge bluff branches snapping and then the most creepy eerie sound I have ever heard it sounded just like an old woman screaming for help hence the name screaming Lou. Most don’t believe that story but every old timer that was raised in the area believes me.

Content:
I had an experience once out hiking in south central Pennsylvania. Used to live out in a hollow, big wooded cliffsides surrounding a creek which cut through creating a valley and a few houses doted alongside its bank with a single road running alongside it. I grew up wandering these woods and considered the stretch my back yard. One day I was climbing up and was suddenly filled with a dmsense of dread more palpitabke than any I've ever experienced in my whole life. I could have sworn I wasn't alone and I called out, saying I would leave and didn't want any trouble. As I headed back I heard noises all around me, and if I stopped these noises would also stop, the forest silent. Haven't been back in that stretch of woods yet.

Author: @JouhouchenHou
Content:
The Appalachian Mountains have long been steeped in mystery and folklore, which has contributed to their reputation as a “creepy” or “forbidden” place in certain cultural narratives. The idea of the Appalachians being a “cursed” or “forbidden” area is not literal in most cases, but symbolic — rooted in history, isolation, and superstition. Here's a breakdown of why this perception exists and continues:


---

1. Ancient and Isolated Geography

The Appalachians are among the oldest mountains on Earth, with a rugged, densely forested terrain that naturally feels ancient and enigmatic.

Remote hollers, fog-covered ridges, and dense woods evoke an eerie feeling — especially at night or during storms.

Many areas remain hard to access, giving rise to a sense of isolation and secrecy.



---

2. Native American Lore and Colonization

Indigenous tribes like the Cherokee considered parts of the Appalachians sacred, while others were believed to be inhabited by spirits or supernatural beings.

Stories of “forbidden lands” often stem from tribal warnings or legends, which were sometimes misunderstood or romanticized by European settlers.



---

3. Folklore and Superstition

Appalachian folklore is rich with ghost stories, witch tales, cryptids (like the Mothman or the Wampus Cat), and omens.

The concept of “the curse” often appears in these tales — old feuds, bloodlines, haunted mines, and cursed cabins.

Oral storytelling traditions preserved these eerie themes, especially in isolated mountain communities.



---

4. Disappearances and Unexplained Events

Some believe the region holds strange energies or phenomena. Cases of hikers disappearing in national parks like the Smoky Mountains have added to the mythos.

Urban legends, like those popularized on TikTok and Reddit (e.g., “don’t go into the woods at night,” “screaming that’s not human”), feed into the idea of the Appalachians as a forbidden zone.



---

5. Modern Media and Internet Lore

The region has inspired horror stories, games (like The Forest and Fallout 76), and online horror communities (e.g., r/Appalachia, r/nosleep).

TikTok and YouTube creators have amplified the idea of supernatural or “government-hidden” happenings, making the mountains seem even more “off-limits.”



---

6. Cultural Misunderstanding

The isolation of Appalachian communities has led outsiders to view them through a lens of suspicion or condescension.

This “othering” contributes to myths of inbreeding, curses, or malevolent hill people — which are unfair stereotypes with real-world harm.



---

Summary

The “creepy curse” and “forbidden” labels attached to the Appalachian Mountains are mostly a blend of:

Ancient terrain

Indigenous legends

Folklore

Isolation

Modern horror storytelling


They're not literally cursed, but they serve as a perfect canvas for mystery and fear in the cultural imagination. If you're interested, I can share specific creepy legends or real-life events from the region.

I was raised in Ohio. One night driving home, i saw something by the side of the road.. about a mile from my home. (The area is very wooded)
Crouched down. Knees bent forward under the chest like a human on all fours. Very pale and smooth. I don't recall the face, the head was just round and smooth.

Just a wooden structure with screens for windows and electricity. Sis was sleeping when the bf woke her up, he heard sniffing outside of the building. Or breathing or whatever. My mom came home late and my sister walked up to the back of the house, maybe.... 30 feet away from the building they were staying in, and bf stayed in the opening of the building. 
He saw -
What he described in the SAME WAY i ddid above - the same creature run past and off into the woods, on all fours, knees bent forward like a human crouched down. 

Ive MAINTAINED that the land there is rotten. (A lot of the area around is built on native burial ground and ceremonial grounds) We have consistently had the WORST LUCK and constant tragedy and heartache in the family. Northeast Ohio, just over the PA state line and a short drive from WV.

Canvas aint stopping anything that wants to get in, metal barbs sure do. Like in those situation I described earlier about things getting oddly quiet and ominous while completely alone, imagine that at night. Author: @brandiewalker265
Content:
One experience I shrugged off as just misremembering as a child, I recently had validated by my cousin who I was with when it happened. My cousins and grandparents live in Sumerco, WV. A very deep holler. I was about 8, while my cousin Jason was probably 11 or 12. We were sitting on a little bridge built on a culvert pipe overlooking a small creek with our legs dangling down just talking about whatever kids talk about. We both watched as a snake swam across the creek but everything suddenly stopped moving. We looked at each other as if simultaneously checking to see if the other had noticed. Looking back down, all time was still seemingly frozen, and in an instant, all was back to normal. 
I saw him this past Easter after over 15 years without seeing each other. We were recounting childhood memories together when I brought it up. He immediately started nodding his head and said he remembered and just always felt it was so odd. I've thought about that moment my entire life and for him to validate it just as I remember it was crazy to me.

Content:
Ive lived in appalachia my whole life, about 5-6 years ago I was working with a bloodhound search group that was searching for a teen that vanished. His mom picked him up from school and when they got home he went around the back of the house and was never seen again. We found his hoodie in the woods and lost all trace. I trained bloodhounds and they are AMAZING at following trails, Multiple dogs at different times followed the same trail to the same spot the hoodie was found and nothing after that.

sidenote: I grew up on the northern end of the mountains in PA and about 10 years ago moved to the southern range in WV. Within this 10 years I have more stories about odd happenings then my entire ~20 years in PA, I am still pretty skeptical on it being something supernatural or alien, but I will say I've heard a large gorilla make its intimidation sounds on my property that is connected to a national forest.... I dont walk around the woods unarmed, but I do still enjoy walking around my property knowing whatever it is, doesnt want anything to do with me.

Some kids went missing and others had a successful life in medicine,  then they claim to have met the little people. In Oklahoma specifically, us Natives had always said to not to talk about them out loud, and worse things will happen if we say their name in our Native language. They do have a lot of significance in Native culture. but I suggest to be wiser and not to talk about them too much!

Content:
That story about the little folk is so interesting, because I am from germany and we have a similar tale here, located not in creepy woods but in the city of cologne:

Long ago in the city of Cologne, there were little house gnomes called the Heinzelmännchen. These tiny, magical creatures would secretly come out at night to help the citizens with their work. They baked bread, cleaned, sewed clothes, and even helped craftsmen with their trades — all while the people slept. Thanks to the Heinzelmännchen, the citizens hardly had to work during the day.

But one day, a curious tailor's wife wanted to see the little helpers for herself. She scattered peas on the floor to make them slip and reveal themselves. That night, the Heinzelmännchen came as usual but tripped over the peas and tumbled all over the place. Angry at being spied on and tricked, they vanished — never to return.

From then on, the people of Cologne had to do their own work again.

Author: @DrMurdercock
Content:
I have been 40 miles any direction from anything even close to civilization in the Appalachian mountains. My grandpa lived in Gate City VA. My dad, myself, Grandpa and my Uncle Red all went out there when I was a kid. 
It was amazing. I remember it being beyond peaceful. You heard NOTHING but nature. You saw no trash....The only trace of man you would find was old arrowheads. We got close and was able to pet wild free roaming ponies. Went to sleep in our tarp tent in spring time on the side of the mountain, woke up with snow on the ground and it was winter.
